item.title: Terry police seek hit and run vehicle that damaged steakhouse - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
TERRY — A vehicle struck and caused extensive damage to the Terry Mercantile Steakhouse Wednesday evening before fleeing the scene, according to the Terry Police Department.

The incident occurred at 6:58 p.m. at the restaurant located at 129 Cunningham Street. The steakhouse, which is currently closed, sustained significant structural damage in the crash.

Surveillance cameras captured footage of what investigators believe may be the suspect vehicle.

Terry police are asking anyone with information about the incident to contact the Terry Police Department or submit a tip anonymously through Crime Stoppers.

item.title: Teen arrested in Gulfport shooting that left man critically injured - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GULFPORT- A Gulfport teenager has been arrested in connection with a Thursday night shooting that left a man critically injured, according to WLOX.

The Gulfport Police Department said John Edward Knight Jr., 17, of Gulfport, was charged with aggravated assault.

Police said the shooting happened in the 3300 block of Martin Luther King Boulevard.

Authorities said a man was shot multiple times and taken to a hospital, where he remained in critical condition.

Knight was taken to the Harrison County Adult Detention Center and was being held on a $250,000 bond, according to WLOX.

Anyone with information about the shooting is asked to call the Gulfport Police Department at 228-868-5959 or Mississippi Coast Crime Stoppers at 877-787-5898.

item.title: Southern Pines takes in 34 pets in one day, asks community for help - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HATTIESBURG – Southern Pines Animal Shelter is asking for donations after taking in 34 pets in one day, including 10 dogs seized from a residential property.

The shelter said its team was called Thursday afternoon to assist Hattiesburg Animal Control with the seizure. When staff arrived, they found crates filled with puppies and dogs.

The animals were taken back to Southern Pines, where they will receive intake exams, food, beds and more spacious kennels, according to the shelter.

In addition to the 10 dogs from the seizure, Southern Pines said it took in 24 other pets Thursday, bringing the day’s total intake to 34 animals.

The shelter said donations help cover medical exams, treatments, food, kennel care, transportation, enrichment, adoption events and other lifesaving programs.

Anyone who wants to help may make a one-time donation or sign up for a monthly gift through Southern Pines Animal Shelter.

item.title: National Park Service urges bear safety precautions ahead of busy summer season - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
STATEWIDE — The National Park Service is urging visitors to take extra precautions in bear country following several recent bear incidents in national parks across the country.

Officials said spring and early summer typically bring increased bear activity as animals search for food, move through habitats and protect cubs.

“National parks are wild places, and wildlife safety is visitor safety,” Jessica Bowron, comptroller exercising the delegated authority of the director, said in a statement. “Simple actions, like giving bears space, securing food and knowing what to do before you enter bear country, can protect visitors and bears.”

The agency encouraged visitors to review park alerts and park-specific bear safety guidance before traveling, noting that bear species, terrain, food storage regulations and bear spray recommendations vary between parks.

The National Park Service recommends visitors never approach bears, stay alert while hiking, travel in groups when possible and make noise in areas with limited visibility, such as near streams or dense vegetation.

Officials also advised visitors to properly store food, trash and scented items and to carry bear spray in parks where it is recommended and permitted.

If a bear is encountered, park officials said visitors should remain calm, speak in a steady voice, slowly back away and avoid sudden movements. Running from a bear is discouraged.

Visitors are also encouraged to report bear encounters to park staff as soon as it is safe to do so.

More information about bear safety is available through individual park websites on the National Park Service website .

item.title: MSDH expands access to substance use disorder treatment statewide - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi State Department of Health has launched a statewide program aimed at expanding access to substance use disorder treatment across all 82 counties.

MSDH said the program is designed to identify risk earlier, reduce barriers to treatment and bring support closer to where patients live.

“This work reflects a simple principle: Substance use disorder care should be available earlier, closer to home, and as part of normal health care, not only after a person reaches crisis,” said Dr. Dan Edney, MSDH executive director and state health officer.

The program uses Epic, MSDH’s electronic health record system, and MyChart to help with screening, intervention and follow-up. Across all 84 MSDH clinics, patients complete an annual screening through MyChart before their visit or on a tablet when they arrive.

MSDH officials said the goal is to help clinicians meet patients at different levels of risk. Patients with low-risk screening results receive positive reinforcement, while clinicians receive guidance through Epic as screening results show greater risk.

Following a six-county pilot program, every county in Mississippi is now using the program. Patients who screen at high risk typically receive follow-up care from addiction specialists through video visits, reducing the need for travel.

MSDH said the program is especially important in Mississippi, where many residents face barriers to care, including transportation challenges, provider shortages and limited access to mental health and substance use treatment.

According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, about 327,000 Mississippians ages 12 and older who needed substance use treatment did not receive it, based on 2022-2023 annual averages.

MSDH said it is one of the few state health departments in the country to provide direct, clinic-based substance use disorder treatment.

Officials said the agency is also exploring ways to safely extend care into the home for eligible patients as more people successfully engage in treatment.

item.title: Meridian Police Investigate Reported Shooting on 5th Street - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Greer Vari
item.description:
MERIDIAN – The Meridian Police Department responded to a 911 call around 11 p.m. Wednesday regarding a reported shooting in the 1600 block of 5th Street.

Officers arrived within minutes and observed a male suffering from a gunshot wound.

Two subjects were taken into custody at the scene, and charges are pending.

Police said the case remains an active and ongoing investigation. Officials also stated the incident is isolated with no ongoing threat to the public.

item.title: MEMA announces Disaster Survivor Assistance Center updates - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Emergency Management Agency has announced updates for Disaster Survivor Assistance Centers and Disaster Recovery Centers under DR-4899.

MEMA said Disaster Survivor Assistance Centers in Carroll, Coahoma, Grenada, Holmes, Montgomery, Quitman, Tallahatchie, Tunica and Yalobusha counties will close at 2 p.m. Saturday, May 16.

Disaster Survivor Assistance Centers in Adams, Bolivar, Claiborne, Issaquena, Jefferson, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren and Washington counties will open at 8 a.m. Monday, May 18.

Disaster Recovery Centers in Alcorn, Benton, Lafayette, Leflore, Panola and Yazoo counties remain open.

MEMA said the application deadline is June 10. All Disaster Recovery Center and Disaster Survivor Assistance locations will close Saturday, May 23.

Officials said receiving disaster assistance benefits will not affect Social Security, Medicare or Medicaid benefits.

item.title: MDWFP honors fallen conservation officers during annual memorial service - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks held its annual Fallen Officer Memorial Service on Thursday, honoring conservation officers who died in the line of duty while protecting Mississippi’s people and natural resources.

The ceremony, held during National Police Week, included remarks from MDWFP Executive Director Lynn Posey and a keynote address and wreath-laying ceremony led by Bill Kinkade, chairman of the House Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks Committee.

“Each year, we gather to remember and honor the brave men and women who gave their lives in the line of duty protecting Mississippi’s people and natural resources,” Posey said in a statement. “This memorial service, taking place during National Police Week, is a reminder of the risks officers face every day and the unwavering commitment they bring to their work.”

MDWFP officials said the memorial serves as a lasting tribute to officers who made the ultimate sacrifice while serving Mississippi’s citizens and conserving the state’s wildlife and natural resources.

item.title: Institute for Marine Mammal Science invites public to endangered sea turtle release in Biloxi - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
BILOXI – The Institute for Marine Mammal Studies is inviting the public to attend a sea turtle release Saturday in Biloxi.

The release is scheduled for 1:30 p.m. in front of Edgewater Mall.

The event comes as IMMS recognizes Endangered Species Day and highlights its work with Kemp’s ridley sea turtles, the most endangered species of sea turtle.

IMMS said the Mississippi Sound is an important habitat for Kemp’s ridley sea turtles, especially juveniles that often come into the organization’s care.

Officials said saving each turtle helps support the species’ population.

item.title: Dog named Asher adopted after 653 days at Corinth-Alcorn Animal Shelter - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
CORINTH – After nearly two years at the Corinth-Alcorn Animal Shelter, Asher has been adopted.

The shelter said Asher spent 653 days in its care before officially finding a forever home.

According to the shelter, Asher was one of 28 dogs rescued from a cruelty case two summers ago. He arrived at the shelter July 30, 2024, scared and uncertain after enduring difficult conditions.

Shelter officials said Asher’s journey shows the importance of patience, care and continued support for animals waiting on adoption.

Asher was adopted by Grady, a shelter volunteer who chose to make him part of his family.

The shelter thanked Grady for giving Asher a home and said dogs like Asher are a reminder of why staff, volunteers and supporters continue their work.

item.title: Both sides rest, judge to hear closing arguments Thursday in Quinton Tellis murder trial - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MONROE, La. — After hearing testimony from a neighbor who said his conscience stopped him from draining a dead woman’s bank account, a lead detective who matched phone records to withdrawals one by one, and a battle of cell phone experts that ultimately changed little, both the state and defense rested their cases in the trial of Quinton Tellis Friday.

Tellis is charged with the murder of Ming Chen “Mandy” Hsiao, who had just finished graduate school in July of 2015 when it appears she was tortured to death, stabbed 31 times. Prosecutors spent the last three days and another week in March building a case that weaves together cell phone tower data, bank records and witness accounts into a portrait of a man who they say killed a woman he just met and then methodically attempted to empty her bank accounts in the days that followed.

Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday before Judge Larry Jefferson, who is presiding over the bench trial. Whether Jefferson will issue a ruling that same day remains unclear.

“A Better Conscience”

Perhaps the most vivid testimony of the day came from Mohammed Mahrous, who lived next door to Tellis’s mother in law on Filhol Avenue in Monroe in 2015. Mahrous, who is currently serving time in Texas on a drug conviction, told the court that one morning Tellis knocked on his door and handed him a debit card with a sticky note on the back.

The note had a PIN number on it, Mahrous said. It started with a 7.

Tellis wanted him to go to the Chase Bank on Highway 165 and withdraw $2,500 in increments of $500 at a time. He said Tellis told him if he brought the money back, he’d be paid for his trouble. Mahrous told the court that the card had an Asian name on it, and a last name that started with an H. It didn’t belong to anyone he knew, and he didn’t recogize the name.

He drove to the bank. ATM photographs entered into evidence placed him there on the morning of July 30, 2015, which was the morning after authorities say evidence shows Hsiao was killed. The photos show he pulled up to the machine and checked the balance. Then, he said, something stopped him.

“A better conscience came to me and told me not to do it,” Mahrous told the court.

Instead of making the withdrawals, he checked the account balance and drove back to return the card to Tellis. He said Tellis got aggressive, calling him a vulgar name, told him he was weak, and told him to give the card to his girlfriend so she could do it instead. Mahrous refused, and told the court he never saw it again.

Monroe police came to his home that fall. He gave a recorded statement, signed a Miranda waiver on September 22, 2015, and submitted to a search of his home, vehicle, cell phone, laptop and DNA.

Tellis, he said, never mentioned the name Mandy or Ming Hsiao.

The defense offered no cross-examination of Mahrous.

Cookson back on the stand

The afternoon belonged to Detective Duane Cookson, the lead investigator in the case, whose testimony walked the court through the physical evidence at the crime scene, the long arc of the investigation, and the painstaking work that ultimately led to a first-degree murder charge.

Cookson was among the first officers at the scene. He found Hsiao’s green iPhone in a blue case approximately three feet from her body, alongside the bed where she lay at the foot. Her hands had blood on them. Cookson said he noticed almost instantly that the phone did not.

When processing the phone, investigators faced a choice between fingerprinting or swabbing for DNA, Cookson said, and since the phone wasn’t bloody, they chose fingerprints but found none belonging to the victim or anyone else.

When detectives searched the apartment on August 8th, they found no cash anywhere inside, not even the $20 that Chase Bank records showed had been withdrawn from Hsiao’s account. That absence took on greater significance after Tellis’s interviews, in which he claimed to have given Hsiao $50 for Lortabs, $25 for a television, and $15 toward a prescription. None of that cash was recovered. The prescription, investigators had learned, was paid by card.

The financial trail Cookson laid out was methodical and thorough. On August 1st, Tellis’s cell phone was placed by cell records in Vicksburg, which was a fact Tellis himself later admitted. During the early morning hours of that date, three transactions were attempted on Hsiao’s Chase account at a Regions Bank ATM. The first was an $800 withdrawal that was declined, then a $400 withdrawal that went through, and another $400 attempt that was declined. Tellis had denied making the withdrawals, even though he could be seen on ATM camera.

On August 7th, his phone called Chase Bank at 11:21 in the morning. That same day, Hsiao’s debit card was used at an Exxon station for $17. When confronted, Tellis produced a new explanation: a man named Kenny whom he described as Hsiao’s “crackhead boyfriend” had been in the car with him and paid for the gas. He had never mentioned Kenny in his August 11th interview, just four days after the transaction. He could not provide Kenny’s last name, address or phone number at the time.

The August 18th and 19th ATM withdrawals from Hsiao’s account brought a new name: “Jay.” Tellis claimed Jay had instructed him to make the withdrawals and paid him in marijuana for his trouble. Investigators had him call Jay right there in the interview room and set up a drug purchase.

Monroe police arrested the man who showed up, and identified him as Termar Key. Key handed over his phone voluntarily, consented to a vehicle search, and had no contact of any kind with Hsiao or her bank accounts. Cookson excluded him as a suspect.

A third name surfaced when Eric Hill, later identified as a cousin of Tellis’s wife, Chiquita Jackson, came to the police station on August 28th and named Curtis Lemons as a suspect. Cookson said he took the tip seriously enough to execute a no-knock warrant on Lemons’s residence within hours. Nothing connecting Lemons to the case was found. Hill later recanted, putting the story squarely on Tellis.

Through it all, Cookson said, Tellis had never once raised either Kenny or Curtis Lemons during his August 11th interview. Both names only appeared after investigators began confronting him with evidence.

The murder charge itself came together slowly. Tellis was initially arrested after his August 19th and 20th interviews only on charges of unauthorized use of an access card and marijuana possession. Cookson testified candidly that he did not yet have probable cause for murder. It was only after he received records from Chase Bank and AT&T and began manually comparing them by cross-referencing every call Tellis’s phone made to Chase with every subsequent transaction on Hsiao’s account that the pattern became undeniable.

Every Chase call preceded a withdrawal, usually within minutes. And before July 29, 2015, Tellis had never called Chase Bank once.

The battle of the experts

Friday morning opened the cross-examination of digital forensics detective Andy Stadius and then testimony from Michael Fegley, a geolocation and cell phone mapping expert called by the defense to challenge the conclusions of Monroe Police Department.

Fegley used a different mapping program than Stadius. It is a controversial system called TRAX, produced by LexisNexis, which generates a different visual representation of cell tower coverage. Where Stadius’s maps showed the familiar wedge shape representing a tower’s sector coverage, Fegley’s program produced what he described as a horizontal plane representation.

The visual difference, however, did not translate into a substantive one. When pressed, Fegley acknowledged that both programs were working from the same AT&T data, the same tower locations, the same sector information, the same location reports.

“My mapping would not conflict with his,” Fegley told the court.

Fegley argued that two location estimates produced during the critical 8:16 to 8:18 p.m. window when calls were made to Chase Bank back-to-back from Hsiao’s phone and then Tellis’s phone on July 29th were geographically inconsistent with each other. He said the distance between them too great to travel in the 25 seconds between reports, meaning at least one of the location estimates must be inaccurate.

But he could not place Tellis’s phone somewhere away from the scene, and he confirmed he was confident the device was in Monroe during the time in question.

The state had also prepared ATF agent Mark Sonnenbecker as an additional cell mapping expert, but after Fegley’s testimony Assistant District Attorney Holly Jones told the court his evidence would be cumulative. He was acknowledged and excused.

Ouachita Corrections phone records

Donna Parks, an IT employee at the Ouachita Correctional Center, testified about the facility’s inmate phone system during the period Tellis was housed there in August 2015. The system flagged 13 calls from Tellis’s pod as possible three-way calls, which are often attempts by an inmate to connect outside parties to a monitored call to avoid detection.

The reason for this is that Eric Hill had testified that Tellis had called him on a three-way call after he had been arrested and said, “You’d better put this on someone else or I’ll F- you up.” This was possibly because Hill testified that Tellis had bragged to him that he had tortured an Asian woman to death for her PIN number to her debit card.

None of the three-way calls were logged under Tellis’s PIN number, Parks said, but she acknowledged that inmates routinely use each other’s PINs, making it impossible to identify or retrieve calls made under another inmate’s number.

Defense Attorney Bob Noel pushed hard against this, asking why the corrections staff couldn’t have caught the three-way call. Jones asked Parks if it would have taken listening to “all the calls” to find that, which Parks confirmed.

The defense pushes back

On cross-examination of Cookson, Noel focused on what the investigation did not find. No DNA belonging to Tellis was recovered from Hsiao’s home. No blood was found in his car. No blood-stained items were seized from his residence or Mahrous’s. He also drew out that Detective Jerry Kent had told Tellis during the August 11th interview that investigators would find his DNA in the bathroom, a statement Cookson acknowledged could be seen as a deliberate falsehood since they didn’t know anything about DNA in the bathroom, a standard tactic in the Reid Technique of interrogation.

On redirect, Jones returned to the bathroom, where Cookson said he observed what appeared to be faint blood on the wall. That blood was tested but produced only a partial DNA profile that could not be fully developed. Jones also noted that if a person had worn gloves no transfer evidence would be expected, and that Tellis had nearly two weeks between the murder and his first interview during which investigators had no knowledge of his movements.

With Cookson’s testimony concluded, the state rested its case. The defense rested without calling additional witnesses. Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday before Judge Larry Jefferson, though whether he will issue a ruling that same day remains unclear.

He said Tellis got aggressive, calling him a vulgar name, told him he was weak, and told him to give the card to his girlfriend so she could do it instead. Mahrous refused, and told the court he never saw it again.

Monroe police came to his home that fall. He gave a recorded statement, signed a Miranda waiver on September 22, 2015, and submitted to a search of his home, vehicle, cell phone, laptop and DNA.

Tellis, he said, never mentioned the name Mandy or Ming Hsiao.

The defense offered no cross-examination of Mahrous.

Cookson back on the stand

The afternoon belonged to Detective Duane Cookson, the lead investigator in the case, whose testimony walked the court through the physical evidence at the crime scene, the long arc of the investigation, and the painstaking work that ultimately led to a first-degree murder charge.

Cookson was among the first officers at the scene. He found Hsiao’s green iPhone in a blue case approximately three feet from her body, alongside the bed where she lay at the foot. Her hands had blood on them. Cookson said he noticed almost instantly that the phone did not.

When processing the phone, investigators faced a choice between fingerprinting or swabbing for DNA, Cookson said, and since the phone wasn’t bloody, they chose fingerprints but found none belonging to the victim or anyone else.

When detectives searched the apartment on August 8th, they found no cash anywhere inside, not even the $20 that Chase Bank records showed had been withdrawn from Hsiao’s account. That absence took on greater significance after Tellis’s interviews, in which he claimed to have given Hsiao $50 for Lortabs, $25 for a television, and $15 toward a prescription. None of that cash was recovered. The prescription, investigators had learned, was paid by card.

The financial trail Cookson laid out was methodical and thorough. On August 1st, Tellis’s cell phone was placed by cell records in Vicksburg, which was a fact Tellis himself later admitted. During the early morning hours of that date, three transactions were attempted on Hsiao’s Chase account at a Regions Bank ATM. The first was an $800 withdrawal that was declined, then a $400 withdrawal that went through, and another $400 attempt that was declined. Tellis had denied making the withdrawals, even though he could be seen on ATM camera.

On August 7th, his phone called Chase Bank at 11:21 in the morning. That same day, Hsiao’s debit card was used at an Exxon station for $17. When confronted, Tellis produced a new explanation: a man named Kenny whom he described as Hsiao’s “crackhead boyfriend” had been in the car with him and paid for the gas. He had never mentioned Kenny in his August 11th interview, just four days after the transaction. He could not provide Kenny’s last name, address or phone number at the time.

The August 18th and 19th ATM withdrawals from Hsiao’s account brought a new name: “Jay.” Tellis claimed Jay had instructed him to make the withdrawals and paid him in marijuana for his trouble. Investigators had him call Jay right there in the interview room and set up a drug purchase.

Monroe police arrested the man who showed up, and identified him as Termar Key. Key handed over his phone voluntarily, consented to a vehicle search, and had no contact of any kind with Hsiao or her bank accounts. Cookson excluded him as a suspect.

A third name surfaced when Eric Hill, later identified as a cousin of Tellis’s wife, Chiquita Jackson, came to the police station on August 28th and named Curtis Lemons as a suspect. Cookson said he took the tip seriously enough to execute a no-knock warrant on Lemons’s residence within hours. Nothing connecting Lemons to the case was found. Hill later recanted, putting the story squarely on Tellis.

Through it all, Cookson said, Tellis had never once raised either Kenny or Curtis Lemons during his August 11th interview. Both names only appeared after investigators began confronting him with evidence.

The murder charge itself came together slowly. Tellis was initially arrested after his August 19th and 20th interviews only on charges of unauthorized use of an access card and marijuana possession. Cookson testified candidly that he did not yet have probable cause for murder. It was only after he received records from Chase Bank and AT&T and began manually comparing them by cross-referencing every call Tellis’s phone made to Chase with every subsequent transaction on Hsiao’s account that the pattern became undeniable.

Every Chase call preceded a withdrawal, usually within minutes. And before July 29, 2015, Tellis had never called Chase Bank once.

The battle of the experts

Friday morning opened the cross-examination of digital forensics detective Andy Stadius and then testimony from Michael Fegley, a geolocation and cell phone mapping expert called by the defense to challenge the conclusions of Monroe Police Department.

Fegley used a different mapping program than Stadius. It is a controversial system called TRAX, produced by LexisNexis, which generates a different visual representation of cell tower coverage. Where Stadius’s maps showed the familiar wedge shape representing a tower’s sector coverage, Fegley’s program produced what he described as a horizontal plane representation.

The visual difference, however, did not translate into a substantive one. When pressed, Fegley acknowledged that both programs were working from the same AT&T data, the same tower locations, the same sector information, the same location reports.

“My mapping would not conflict with his,” Fegley told the court.

Fegley argued that two location estimates produced during the critical 8:16 to 8:18 p.m. window when calls were made to Chase Bank back-to-back from Hsiao’s phone and then Tellis’s phone on July 29th were geographically inconsistent with each other. He said the distance between them too great to travel in the 25 seconds between reports, meaning at least one of the location estimates must be inaccurate.

But he could not place Tellis’s phone somewhere away from the scene, and he confirmed he was confident the device was in Monroe during the time in question.

The state had also prepared ATF agent Mark Sonnenbecker as an additional cell mapping expert, but after Fegley’s testimony Assistant District Attorney Holly Jones told the court his evidence would be cumulative. He was acknowledged and excused.

Ouachita Corrections phone records

Donna Parks, an IT employee at the Ouachita Correctional Center, testified about the facility’s inmate phone system during the period Tellis was housed there in August 2015. The system flagged 13 calls from Tellis’s pod as possible three-way calls, which are often attempts by an inmate to connect outside parties to a monitored call to avoid detection.

The reason for this is that Eric Hill had testified that Tellis had called him on a three-way call after he had been arrested and said, “You’d better put this on someone else or I’ll F- you up.” This was possibly because Hill testified that Tellis had bragged to him that he had tortured an Asian woman to death for her PIN number to her debit card.

None of the three-way calls were logged under Tellis’s PIN number, Parks said, but she acknowledged that inmates routinely use each other’s PINs, making it impossible to identify or retrieve calls made under another inmate’s number.

Defense Attorney Bob Noel pushed hard against this, asking why the corrections staff couldn’t have caught the three-way call. Jones asked Parks if it would have taken listening to “all the calls” to find that, which Parks confirmed.

The defense pushes back

On cross-examination of Cookson, Noel focused on what the investigation did not find. No DNA belonging to Tellis was recovered from Hsiao’s home. No blood was found in his car. No blood-stained items were seized from his residence or Mahrous’s. He also drew out that Detective Jerry Kent had told Tellis during the August 11th interview that investigators would find his DNA in the bathroom, a statement Cookson acknowledged could be seen as a deliberate falsehood since they didn’t know anything about DNA in the bathroom, a standard tactic in the Reid Technique of interrogation.

On redirect, Jones returned to the bathroom, where Cookson said he observed what appeared to be faint blood on the wall. That blood was tested but produced only a partial DNA profile that could not be fully developed. Jones also noted that if a person had worn gloves no transfer evidence would be expected, and that Tellis had nearly two weeks between the murder and his first interview during which investigators had no knowledge of his movements.

With Cookson’s testimony concluded, the state rested its case. The defense rested without calling additional witnesses. Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday before Judge Larry Jefferson, though whether he will issue a ruling that same day remains unclear.

item.title: Thursday Weather: Sunshine and warm temps - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Mary Apel
item.description:
Good morning! We’re settling into a really nice stretch of weather across Mississippi, with warm temperatures, lots of sunshine and very little chance for rain through the rest of the week.

Today will be sunny with a high around 83 degrees and light northeast winds at 5 to 10 miles per hour. Humidity stays fairly comfortable this afternoon, and rain chances are almost nonexistent at just 2 percent. Tonight will be partly cloudy and pleasant, with lows dipping to around 59 degrees.

Looking ahead, temperatures will continue to warm under mostly sunny to sunny skies. Highs will generally stay in the low to mid-80s for the next few days before some areas start pushing close to 90 degrees by late week. Overnight lows will also trend warmer heading into the weekend and into next week.

The good news is the dry pattern is expected to hold through the weekend, with the next meaningful rain chances likely holding off until early next week. So if you’ve got outdoor plans, it’s shaping up to be a great stretch of weather to enjoy.

item.title: Texas man pleads guilty in federal cocaine trafficking case tied to 19 defendants - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
GREENVILLE — A Texas man pleaded guilty Tuesday in federal court in connection with a large-scale drug trafficking investigation that resulted in the seizure of more than 25 kilograms of cocaine, approximately $150,000 in drug proceeds and multiple vehicles, according to federal officials.

Harold Cook, 55, of Fort Worth, Texas, entered the guilty plea after a federal jury had already been selected in the case, prosecutors said.

According to court documents, Cook and his co-defendants were charged in an indictment that included cocaine conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime and possession with intent to distribute cocaine.

His co-defendants include:

Cook will be sentenced later by Chief U.S. District Judge Debra M. Brown. He was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service following his guilty plea.

Federal officials said the investigation was part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative established in 2025 to target criminal cartels, human smuggling operations and drug trafficking organizations.

“We are all aware of the devastation that drug trafficking and violent gangs have visited on our communities,” Scott F. Leary, U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Mississippi, said in a statement. “By dismantling this drug trafficking organization, hundreds of pounds of drugs will be taken off our streets and lives will be saved.”

Leary praised the work of the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Department, along with DEA offices in Oxford, El Paso and Fairview Heights, Illinois, as well as the United States Marshals Service.

Steven Hofer, special agent in charge of the DEA, said the operation demonstrated cooperation between federal, state and local agencies.

“We are sending a clear message that criminal organizations have no place in Mississippi,” Hofer said.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sam Stringfellow and Julie Addison.

item.title: STEPPING UP TO SERVE: Pure Air Consultants, Hometown Magazines provide HVAC system to young family in need - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Pure Air Consultants , a local, family-owned HVAC company, in partnership with Hometown Magazines, recently provided a new heating and cooling system to a young local family through the company’s PAC Gives Back initiative.

The recipient family is a newlywed couple, ages 21 and 22, who have taken in their nephew and are working to build a stable home for him.

Through the giveaway, the family received a new 14 SEER Day & Night heating and cooling system installed by Pure Air Consultants. The company said the initiative was created as a way to give back to the community that has supported its growth over the years.

Pure Air Consultants announced the program earlier this year, seeking nominations for individuals or families in Hinds, Madison and Rankin counties who were in need of a new heating and cooling system but could not afford to replace an old or inefficient unit.

Company representatives said the giveaway was intended to help a family facing hardship while also recognizing the importance of safe and reliable home comfort.

Pure Air Consultants partnered with Hometown Magazines to help promote the initiative and encourage nominations from across the metro Jackson area.

The company said providing the system to the selected family was a meaningful opportunity to support a household working to care for a child and create a secure home environment.

Pure Air Consultants is a locally owned and operated HVAC company that offers heating and cooling services, duct cleaning, UV lights and air purifiers.

Check out the heartwarming video that Hometown Magazine put together when they surprised the young family.

item.title: Ridgeland to host Memorial Day ceremony, America250 exhibit - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
RIDGELAND — The City of Ridgeland will host a Memorial Day ceremony and unveil a new America250 exhibit on May 21 at Ridgeland City Hall.

The park features memorial benches and plaques honoring the six branches of the U.S. military, along with the Walk of Heroes, a flagpole and a seven-foot bell tower.

Retired Brig. Gen. Joe Hargett will deliver keynote remarks during the ceremony. Gene McGee, mayor of Ridgeland, and Col. John McCollum are also scheduled to speak.

The program will include a presentation of colors by the Ridgeland High School AFJROTC, along with music from the National Guard Band and Dr. Catherine Sledge.

Following the ceremony, attendees will be invited to tour a new America250 exhibit curated by Nancy Batson, chair of the City History Committee.

Chaplain David Morris and members of the Ridgeland Board of Aldermen and other city officials are also expected to participate.

item.title: Mississippi Museum of Natural Science named Best Museum in Mississippi - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Museum of Natural Science has been named Best Museum in Mississippi in Mississippi Magazine’s Best of Mississippi 2026 Reader Poll, officials announced this week.

More information is available through the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science website.

item.title: Mexican national sentenced to more than 10 years in child exploitation case in Mississippi - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
ABERDEEN — A Mexican national living illegally in the United States has been sentenced to more than 10 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to distributing and receiving child sexual abuse material through Facebook Messenger, federal officials announced.

Adolfo Raul Vasquez-Santana, 32, of Southaven, was sentenced to 121 months in prison, followed by five years of supervised release. Senior U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock also ordered him to pay $14,000 in restitution to victims.

According to court documents, Vasquez-Santana downloaded and shared violent videos depicting the sexual abuse of children through the messaging platform Facebook Messenger.

The investigation began after the Southaven Police Department received a tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Homeland Security Investigations later determined Vasquez-Santana was in the country illegally and pursued federal charges.

Officials with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement have placed an immigration detainer on Vasquez-Santana, meaning he is expected to be removed from the United States after serving his federal sentence.

“Child pornography is a plague,” Scott F. Leary, U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Mississippi, said in a statement. “Children are victimized not only through the production of obscene material, but through its continual distribution.”

Leary also praised the work of Southaven police, Homeland Security Investigations and Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Addison, who prosecuted the case.

Matt Wright, acting special agent in charge for HSI New Orleans, said investigators acted quickly after receiving information about the defendant.

“HSI is committed to protecting children from predators who use technology to exploit them,” Wright said. “We remain vigilant against child predators and will continue to pursue these offenders wherever they operate.”

Federal officials said the case was part of both Operation Take Back America and Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide Department of Justice initiative aimed at combating online child sexual exploitation.

item.title: McComb man arrested in Vicksburg on child sex crime charges - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PIKE COUNTY – A McComb man was arrested Wednesday morning in Vicksburg on child sex crime charges.

The Pike County Sheriff’s Office said Sheriff Wally Jones, along with Pike County investigators and deputies and investigators from the Warren County Sheriff’s Office, arrested Christopher Scott Landrum around 7 a.m. May 13.

Landrum was charged with one count of sexual battery and one count of enticing a minor child, according to the sheriff’s office.

Jones said his office will continue pursuing people accused of targeting children in Pike County, no matter where they are located.

“I’ve been very clear to anybody who has criminal intentions in Pike County, especially those who target children — you do not have a safe haven in Pike County,” Jones said.

Jones thanked Pike County investigators and the Warren County Sheriff’s Office for their help in the case.

The sheriff’s office is asking any additional victims related to the case to come forward and contact the Pike County Sheriff’s Office.

All suspects are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

item.title: Man sentenced to 15 years day-for-day in meth trafficking case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
A man has been sentenced to serve 15 years in prison after pleading guilty to trafficking methamphetamine, according to the First Circuit Court District Attorney’s Office.

District Attorney Jason Herring said Dale Wayne Griggs pleaded guilty May 14 before Circuit Court Judge Michael P. Mills Jr.

Mills sentenced Griggs to 40 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections, with 25 years suspended, leaving 15 years to serve.

Because of the nature of the charge, Griggs must serve the 15-year sentence day-for-day without the possibility of parole or early release, according to the district attorney’s office.

After his release, Griggs will be required to complete five years of post-release supervision.

The case was investigated by the North Mississippi Narcotics Unit.

item.title: Expert qualifications, flood of objections mark chaotic day in Tellis bench trial - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MONROE, La. — What seemingly should have been a straightforward presentation of cell phone evidence turned into a prolonged battle over expert qualifications and a flood of defense objections Thursday in the bench trial of Quinton Tellis, charged in the 2015 death of University of Louisiana Monroe grad school graduate Ming Chen “Mandy” Hsiao.

At the center of Thursday’s proceedings was a fight over cell phone location evidence that prosecutors say places Tellis at the scene of Hsiao’s death on July 29, 2015, a window prosecutors have bookended between 7:41 p.m., the timestamp of her last Facebook message, and 8:16 p.m., when records show Tellis’s phone calling the Chase Bank customer service number and entering her account and PIN.

The Prosecution’s Expert

The prosecution called Monroe Police Department Detective Andy Stadius, a 17-year law enforcement veteran and lead digital analyst for the Western Louisiana Violent Offender Task Force, a U.S. Marshals Service task force. Stadius spent six and a half years with MPD before joining the task force, and previously worked for ULM and the Ouachita Parish Sheriff’s Department.

His credentials include training as a U.S. Army geospatial intelligence imagery analyst, a role the Army describes as analyzing aerial imagery, geospatial data, full motion video and electronic monitoring to determine precise target coordinates and identify enemy positions. He is also certified through Nighthawk, one of the most widely used and court-validated cell data analysis platforms in the country, and works with the Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence, or SWGDE, a nonprofit that brings together law enforcement, legal professionals and private industry to establish standards for digital evidence.

In spite of his military designation through the Army School of Geospatial Intelligence that qualifies him to use geolocation in service of the American government, the defense challenged Stadius’s qualifications as a geolocation expert. After argument that left the court uncertain about the technical distinctions involved, the judge declined to certify him in that specific area. He was instead qualified as an expert in digital forensics, cellular data analysis and digital evidence interpretation.

The ruling meany Stadius could testify about what the call records show, which towers Tellis’s phone connected to, when, and the pattern of activity in the data, but his ability to render a precise geographic opinion about where the phone was physically located is limited.

19 Objections

The defense raised 19 objections to the state’s cell phone evidence presentation, material the defense has had in its possession for months. The volume and timing of the objections interrupted testimony for a significant amount of the day and forced the court to work through complex technical disputes almost on the fly.

Assistant District Attorney Holly Jones noted during the objections that it “would have been nice” if they had been raised in a motion in limine prior to trial. A motion in limine is a pretrial motion asking the court to rule on the admissibility of specific evidence before proceedings begin, allowing complex disputes to be resolved with adequate time for argument and research rather than in the middle of testimony.

Jones’s comment reflected her frustration that disputes over technical evidence the defense has had for months were being litigated in real time, interrupting the flow of the trial and forcing the judge to make rulings on highly technical material without the benefit of full briefing.

The defense appeared to be working aggressively to prevent testimony about cell phone data that prosecutors say places Tellis at the scene of Hsiao’s death. So far, the defense has offered no indication whether it has evidence placing Tellis anywhere else at the time she is believed to have been killed.

Scheduling Complications Loom

The battle over objections has created what could end up being significant scheduling complications. A Nighthawk expert who traveled to Monroe specifically to testify was in the courtroom Thursday but must fly out Friday. The prosecution had mentioned Wednesday that they needed to put him on the stand Thursday, but the day’s proceedings prevented that. He will need to testify early Friday if he is to testify at all.

Meanwhile, Detective Duane Cookson, who has provided extensive testimony about the investigative interviews, the witnesses, the bank records and cell data at the heart of the case, has not yet been released from the stand and has not been cross-examined by the defense.

What Stadius Testified

The prosecution questioned Stadius Thursday, though court let out before the defense could cross-examine him. He used his analysis of AT&T call detail records, NELOS location events and data sessions from Tellis’s phone, and walked the court through a methodology built on verified locations and times, to establish how Tellis’s phone interacted with the cellular network on key dates.

On July 27, 2015, two days before Hsiao’s death, a witness placed Tellis at her apartment complex on Filhiol Avenue. Cell records from that day show his phone connecting to towers consistent with that area during the times the witness described, as well as hitting a different tower consistent with a Walmart location during a time where records show he was present that afternoon.

The most significant testimony centered on the evening of July 29, 2015. Stadius told the court that Hsiao’s phone was used to attempt two calls to an AT&T customer service number at 8:16 p.m., both of which failed.

Within seconds and in the same minute, Tellis’s phone successfully completed a call to that same number, lasting one minute and six seconds. Moments later, the number 7223, identified as Hsiao’s Chase Bank PIN, was manually entered on Tellis’s device. His phone then called Chase Bank a second time at 8:18 p.m.

On Wednesday, Cookson testified to a day planner belonging to Hsiao that had the number 7223 linked to multiple account passwords such as power, water, and other things.

Cell tower data during that window showed Tellis’s phone connecting to towers in the general area of Hsiao’s Filhiol Avenue apartment, though Stadius was careful throughout his testimony to note that the data establishes the phone’s general location, not its precise placement or who was holding it.

Stadius also testified that Hsiao’s own digital activity effectively stopped on July 29. Her last self-initiated phone call was at 5:22 p.m. Her last Facebook Messenger activity was around 7:41 p.m. After the 8:16 p.m. Chase call, which Stadius said he could not specifically attribute to Hsiao or Tellis, there was no further user-initiated activity on her phone until it was collected by Monroe police on Aug. 8.

Meanwhile, Stadius testified that Hsiao had never dialed a 1 before 800 or any other area code in the history of her phone records, but the calls to Chase Bank had a 1 in front of them. In addition, her phone had always had “events,” or interactions with towers on every day until July 29, when it went silent until detectives found it next to her body.

In the 10 days that the prosecution holds fell between her death and the discovery of her body, seven calls had gone to voice mail. Between June 1 and July 29, only 13 calls had gone to voice mail in total.

In the days and weeks following her death, Chase Bank records show Hsiao’s debit card was used at a Regions Bank ATM in Vicksburg in the early morning hours of Aug. 1, and at a Chase Bank branch at 1200 Sterlington Road in Monroe on Aug. 17, 18 and 19. Cell records place Tellis’s phone in the area of each of those transactions at the times they occurred. ATM photographs obtained from Chase were also presented to corroborate the cell data.

ADA Jones, who conducted the examination, preemptively addressed the limitations of the evidence in her questioning, with Stadius confirming he cannot say definitively where Tellis himself was at any given time, only that the device associated with his phone number was in the general area reflected by the tower data.

Stadius had not been cross-examined by the defense when court let out for the day at 6:45 p.m. Trial resumes Friday at 9 a.m. and could conceivably go through Saturday as well.

item.title: Corinth man accused of falsely reporting bomb in towed vehicle in Tupelo - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TUPELO – A Corinth man was arrested after Tupelo police said he falsely reported having a bomb in a vehicle.

The Tupelo Police Department said officers were notified May 11 that a person had reported to Lee County 911 that he had a bomb in his vehicle, which had previously been towed.

Police said officers found the suspect at North Mississippi Medical Center, located at 830 S. Gloster St., where he was arrested for public intoxication.

After further investigation, Allen T. Morgan, 61, of Corinth, was charged May 12 with one count of false reporting of a bomb or explosive device.

Tupelo Municipal Court Judge Allen ordered Morgan held on a $5,000 bond.

The case will be presented to the Lee County grand jury.

item.title: 33-year-old Taylorsville man killed in Perry County crash - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PERRY COUNTY – A Taylorsville man was killed Wednesday afternoon in a crash in Perry County, according to the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

MHP said the crash happened around 2:43 p.m. May 13 on Mississippi Highway 29.

A 2018 Cadillac XT5 driven by Georgene F. Watkins, 79, of Petal, was traveling west on Daughtry Hill Road when it collided with a 2013 Volvo semi-truck traveling south on Mississippi Highway 29, authorities said.

The semi-truck was driven by Darrell Sullivan, 33, of Taylorsville.

Watkins was taken to a local hospital with minor injuries. Sullivan suffered fatal injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene by the Perry County Coroner’s Office.

The crash remains under investigation by the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

item.title: 13 arrested after vandalism reported at North Panola High School - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PANOLA COUNTY – Several people were arrested after North Panola High School was found severely damaged earlier this week, according to the Panola County Sheriff’s Office.

Deputies were dispatched to the school, located on Highway 51 North in Sardis, in the early morning hours of May 12.

When deputies arrived, they found severe damage throughout much of the building, authorities said. Multiple fire extinguishers had been discharged, classrooms were damaged and the principal’s office had been broken into and damaged.

Investigators spent much of Tuesday gathering evidence and identifying suspects. Adult suspects were booked into the Panola County Detention Center. Juvenile suspects were released to the custody of their parents or legal guardians and will be adjudicated through youth court.

Those arrested include Jamarion Armstrong, 18; Aaliyah House, 21; Jmarion Lamar, 18; Charles Clark, 18; Makiya Lockett, 18; Darrell Miller, 18; Antarria Mosley, 19; Denard Presley, 18; Willie Rucker, 18; Pheghton Spann, 18; Anijah Taylor, 18; Tony Wren, 20; and Dominic Young, 18.

Authorities said charges are pending, and more charges and suspects may be forthcoming as the investigation continues.

item.title: Two MDOC agents honored among Mississippi ‘Top Cops’ - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON- Two Mississippi Department of Corrections agents were among 66 law enforcement officers recognized as “Top Cops” during the 20th annual Police Memorial and Appreciation Day event.

Jacob Wilson and Jonah Fields, both with MDOC’s Corrections Investigation Division, were honored Tuesday at the Mississippi Trade Mart at the State Fairgrounds.

The honorees included 18 recipients from state agencies, 41 municipal and county recipients and seven federal recipients. Two sheriff’s deputies from Hinds and Jackson counties who died in the line of duty in 2025 also were honored.

Fields has served with MDOC for five years and eight months. He previously worked as a probation and parole agent before joining the Corrections Investigation Division, where he has served for the past two years.

“Receiving this award is a reflection of the CID as a unit that remains committed to public safety, and the safety of the individuals in the custody of MDOC,” Fields said.

Wilson is a third-generation law enforcement officer with 12 years and 10 months of experience with MDOC. He also previously served as a probation and parole agent before moving to CID, where he has served for the past five years. Overall, Wilson has spent 15 years and nine months in law enforcement.

Wilson said he was surprised to be nominated for the award.

“This was very unexpected. I am usually the one recommending other agents for promotions and awards for their work and achievements. I am very humbled,” Wilson said.

item.title: Two arrested for allegedly stealing used cooking oil from Perry County restaurant - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PERRY COUNTY – Two people have been arrested in connection with the theft of used cooking oil from a Perry County restaurant.

The Perry County Sheriff’s Department said deputies arrested Wesley Dion Chen, 39, of New York, and Huang Zhong Hui, 37, of Pennsylvania, on Monday, May 11.

Both were charged with two counts of malicious mischief and larceny.

Authorities said Chen and Hui were identified as the people involved in stealing used cooking oil from the Catfish Wagon Restaurant on two separate occasions. Used cooking oil is commonly sold to certain locations for recycling.

The sheriff’s department said other law enforcement agencies are investigating similar incidents in other jurisdictions and possible links between the cases.

Sheriff Jacob Garner thanked Perry County residents for helping locate and identify the suspects.

“Me and my team will continue working hard to identify, locate, and arrest individuals who choose to come into Perry County and steal from our hardworking citizens,” Garner said.

item.title: Paden man arrested on drug charges after Tishomingo County checkpoint - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TISHOMINGO COUNTY – A Paden man was arrested on drug charges after deputies said he stopped suddenly near a safety checkpoint and later hit a patrol vehicle.

The Tishomingo County Sheriff’s Department said deputies were conducting a safety checkpoint around 8:30 p.m. May 8 on County Road 169 near County Road 166.

Deputies said they saw a Honda Accord traveling south on County Road 169 when the driver slammed on the brakes and swerved partially off the roadway before stopping about 40 yards from deputies. Another southbound vehicle also slammed on its brakes behind the Accord, nearly hitting it, according to the sheriff’s department.

Deputies told the driver to pull off the roadway. While doing so, the driver struck a stationary patrol vehicle that had its blue lights activated, authorities said.

The driver was identified as Jacob Earl Hill of Paden.

Deputies said they later recovered a plastic bag that had been thrown into a ditch. Inside the bag, deputies found about 29 grams of suspected methamphetamine and about 4 grams of suspected cocaine.

Deputies also reported finding one dosage unit of oxycodone inside the Accord.

Hill was arrested and charged with possession of a Schedule II controlled substance, methamphetamine, 10 to 30 grams; possession of a Schedule II controlled substance, cocaine, 2 to 10 grams; possession of a Schedule II controlled substance, less than two dosage units; and several misdemeanor traffic violations.

Judge Seth Adams set Hill’s bond at $40,000.

item.title: Fitch announces 23 arrests, six ICE detainers after Fentanyl Strike Force operations - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced the completion of two recent Fentanyl Strike Force operations that resulted in 23 arrests and six ICE detainers.

The operations were conducted April 30 in Corinth and May 7 in Meridian, according to Fitch’s office.

“We are grateful to work alongside such dedicated and skilled federal, state, and local law enforcement partners,” Fitch said. “Together, we are taking dangerous criminals off the streets and restoring peace and security in our communities.”

Participating agencies included the Alcorn County Sheriff’s Office, Corinth Police Department, Commercial Transportation Enforcement Division, East Mississippi Narcotics Task Force, Homeland Security Investigations, Lauderdale County Sheriff’s Office, Mississippi Alcoholic Beverage Control, Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics, Mississippi Highway Patrol, Tishomingo County Sheriff’s Office and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Fitch announced the creation of the Fentanyl Strike Force in 2023 along with the launch of her One Pill Can Kill public education and awareness campaign.

Through the strike force, more than 800 law enforcement officers have been trained to safely handle fentanyl and investigate narcotics cases, according to the attorney general’s office. A recent training in Corinth preceded the operation there.

Fitch’s office said the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office was the first agency in the state to sign up as an ICE 287(g) Task Force partner and the first to complete Task Force enforcement action in Mississippi. The office said all sworn AGO law enforcement officers are trained and certified under the program.

Under the ICE Section 287(g) program, state and local law enforcement agencies may partner with ICE for delegated immigration enforcement related to public safety, including identifying people, lodging immigration detainers and initiating removal proceedings for potentially deportable people booked into jail facilities.

BYRAM – Multiple people were arrested as part of an ongoing Byram police operation aimed at reducing illegal drug activity and violent crime.

The Byram Police Department said the arrests were made through its “Operation Keep Byram Safe” initiative.

Police said Khamari Alexander was arrested on two counts of possession of a controlled substance, possession of a firearm by a felon and tampering with evidence.

Angel Smoot also was arrested and charged with possession of a controlled substance, methamphetamine, and possession of a Schedule II controlled substance.

The department said the arrests are part of continued targeted enforcement efforts to enhance public safety in Byram.

All suspects are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
